Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: Mitigating Content Effects on Reasoning in Language Models through Fine-Grained Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can content biases in reasoning be mitigated through activation steering in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces K-CAST, a fine-grained conditional activation steering method that effectively reduces content biases in reasoning, improving formal reasoning accuracy by up to 15%.
papers.conclusion: Activation-level interventions offer a scalable inference-time strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive steering methods enable linear control over content biases in reasoning.
Static steering is insufficient to debias all tested models.
K-CAST reduces biases on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy.
Steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations and incurs minimal side effects on multilingual language modeling capabilities.
Steering vectors can partially generalize to different out-of-distribution reasoning tasks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are performed on LLMs of up to 9 billion parameters due to computational constraints.
The study focuses mainly on synthetically generated tasks, which may not fully capture real-world applications.
future_direction: Applying the steering methodology to larger models.
Assessing how steering for content effect can impact real-world applications in critical domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently demonstrate reasoning limitations, often conflating content plausibility (i.e., material inference) with logical validity (i.e., formal inference). This can result in biased inferences, where plausible arguments are incorrectly deemed logically valid or vice versa. Mitigating this limitation is critical, as it undermines the trustworthiness and generalizability of LLMs in applications that demand rigorous logical consistency. This paper investigates the problem of mitigating content biases on formal reasoning through activation steering. Specifically, we curate a controlled syllogistic reasoning dataset to disentangle formal validity from content plausibility. After localising the layers responsible for formal and material inference, we investigate contrastive activation steering methods for test-time interventions. An extensive empirical analysis on different LLMs reveals that contrastive steering consistently supports linear control over content biases. However, we observe that a static approach is insufficient for improving all the tested models. We then leverage the possibility to control content effects by dynamically determining the value of the steering parameters via fine-grained conditional methods. We found that conditional steering is effective on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy with a newly introduced kNN-based method (K-CAST). Finally, additional experiments reveal that steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations, incurs minimal side effects on language modeling capabilities, and can partially generalize to out-of-distribution reasoning tasks. Practically, this paper demonstrates that activation-level interventions can offer a scalable strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased formal reasoning.

papers.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in Transformers work? The paper hypothesizes that Transformers implement gradient descent in their forward pass to learn from in-context data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers trained on auto-regressive objectives implement gradient descent in their forward pass, providing a mechanistic understanding of in-context learning for regression tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning in Transformers can be understood as gradient descent in the forward pass, at least for regression tasks, providing a mechanistic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
A single linear self-attention layer can be constructed to perform one step of gradient descent on a linear regression loss.
When trained on linear regression tasks, linear self-attention-only Transformers converge to weights that match the gradient descent construction.
Multiple layers of self-attention can implement multiple steps of gradient descent and even surpass plain gradient descent by learning a curvature correction (GD++).
Transformers with MLPs can solve nonlinear regression tasks by learning linear models on deep representations.
The paper connects the induction head mechanism to in-context learning by gradient descent.
papers.limitation:
The findings on linear self-attention-only Transformers only explain a limited part of a complex process, and it may be one of many possible methods giving rise to in-context learning.
The analysis is limited to regression tasks and simple Transformer architectures.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to language modeling and other domains.
Investigating the role of softmax and LayerNorm in in-context learning.
Exploring the connection to hypernetworks and weight generation.
papers.abstract: At present, the mechanisms of in-context learning in Transformers are not well understood and remain mostly an intuition. In this paper, we suggest that training Transformers on auto-regressive objectives is closely related to gradient-based meta-learning formulations. We start by providing a simple weight construction that shows the equivalence of data transformations induced by 1) a single linear self-attention layer and by 2) gradient-descent (GD) on a regression loss. Motivated by that construction, we show empirically that when training self-attention-only Transformers on simple regression tasks either the models learned by GD and Transformers show great similarity or, remarkably, the weights found by optimization match the construction. Thus we show how trained Transformers become mesa-optimizers i.e. learn models by gradient descent in their forward pass. This allows us, at least in the domain of regression problems, to mechanistically understand the inner workings of in-context learning in optimized Transformers. Building on this insight, we furthermore identify how Transformers surpass the performance of plain gradient descent by learning an iterative curvature correction and learn linear models on deep data representations to solve non-linear regression tasks. Finally, we discuss intriguing parallels to a mechanism identified to be crucial for in-context learning termed induction-head (Olsson et al., 2022) and show how it could be understood as a specific case of in-context learning by gradient descent learning within Transformers. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at https://github.com/google-research/self-organising-systems/tree/master/transformers_learn_icl_by_gd .

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Interpretation of Multi-Step Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models perform multi-step reasoning tasks by using a reasoning mechanism or by memorizing answers from pretraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MechanisticProbe, a probing method that recovers reasoning trees from attention patterns, providing evidence that LMs perform multi-step reasoning mechanistically.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that reasoning trees can often be detected from LM attention patterns, supporting the claim that LMs may reason mechanistically.
papers.key_findings:
MechanisticProbe can recover reasoning trees from attention patterns of GPT-2 and LLaMA for most examples.
LMs identify useful statements in bottom layers and perform reasoning steps in higher layers.
Pruning attention heads that contribute to reasoning tree detection degrades performance, indicating a causal role.
Higher probing scores correlate with higher model accuracy and robustness to noise.
Finetuned models show clearer reasoning patterns in attention than few-shot models.
papers.limitation:
The study considered fairly simple reasoning tasks.
The analysis averages over attention heads, but heads may have different functions, especially in shallow models.
The analysis is limited to single-token prediction tasks and does not cover chain-of-thought reasoning.
future_direction: Explore more challenging reasoning tasks.
Analyze reasoning in chain-of-thought prompting settings.
papers.abstract: Yifan Hou, Jiaoda Li, Yu Fei, Alessandro Stolfo, Wangchunshu Zhou, Guangtao Zeng, Antoine Bosselut, Mrinmaya Sachan. Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2023.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Unveiling Transformers with LEGO: a synthetic reasoning task
papers.research_question: How do Transformer architectures learn to follow a chain of reasoning, and how do architectural choices (like weight tying) and data composition (like pretraining) affect their generalization and the emergence of specific attention patterns?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the LEGO synthetic reasoning task to study how Transformers learn to follow chains of reasoning. It identifies that successful models develop specialized attention heads for association (long-range identity matching) and manipulation (short-range operations), and based on this insight, proposes the LEGO attention module which reduces FLOPs while maintaining or improving performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.conclusion: The LEGO task provides a controlled setting to understand how Transformers learn reasoning, revealing the importance of structured attention patterns for generalization. These insights can guide architectural design, as demonstrated by the proposed LEGO attention module which offers efficiency gains.
papers.key_findings:
Classical generalization can be deceptive, as models can learn 'shortcut' solutions that do not follow the intended chain of reasoning and impede out-of-distribution generalization.
Iterative architectures like ALBERT, which share weights across layers, exhibit better length extrapolation (generalization to longer reasoning chains) than non-iterative architectures like BERT, suggesting an inductive bias towards implementing a 'for-loop'.
Pretraining helps generalization on the LEGO task primarily by providing a beneficial initialization with structured attention patterns (association and manipulation heads), rather than by encoding complex task-specific knowledge.
Models can be incentivized to learn more robust, iterative solutions through techniques like stochastic depth training, which improves length extrapolation.
The identified structured attention patterns motivate a new LEGO attention module, which when used as a drop-in replacement for standard attention, reduces computational cost and matches or improves performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.limitation: The study uses a synthetic task, which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world reasoning tasks.
future_direction: Applying the insights from the LEGO task to currently challenging mathematical reasoning tasks like MATH and IsarStep.
Exploring the application of the LEGO attention module to other domains and tasks.
papers.abstract: We propose a synthetic reasoning task, LEGO (Learning Equality and Group Operations), that encapsulates the problem of following a chain of reasoning, and we study how the Transformer architectures learn this task. We pay special attention to data effects such as pretraining (on seemingly unrelated NLP tasks) and dataset composition (e.g., differing chain length at training and test time), as well as architectural variants such as weight-tied layers or adding convolutional components. We study how the trained models eventually succeed at the task, and in particular, we manage to understand some of the attention heads as well as how the information flows in the network. In particular, we have identified a novel \emph{association} pattern that globally attends only to identical tokens. Based on these observations we propose a hypothesis that here pretraining helps for LEGO tasks due to certain structured attention patterns, and we experimentally verify this hypothesis. We also observe that in some data regime the trained transformer finds ``shortcut" solutions to follow the chain of reasoning, which impedes the model's robustness, and moreover we propose ways to prevent it. Motivated by our findings on structured attention patterns, we propose the LEGO attention module, a drop-in replacement for vanilla attention heads. This architectural change significantly reduces Flops and maintains or even \emph{improves} the model's performance at large-scale pretraining.

papers.title: Under the Shadow of Babel: How Language Shapes Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Do different languages lead LLMs to think differently? Do LLMs internalize the cognitive biases embedded in different languages, specifically in causal reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BICAUSE, a structured bilingual dataset for causal reasoning, and provides empirical evidence that LLMs internalize language-specific reasoning biases, showing typologically aligned attention patterns and a shared understanding when reasoning succeeds.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit language-specific biases in causal reasoning that impact performance, but when reasoning succeeds, they form a shared understanding that transcends surface linguistic form.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit typologically aligned attention patterns, focusing more on causes and sentence-initial connectives in Chinese, while showing a more balanced distribution in English.
Models internalize language-specific preferences for causal word order and often rigidly apply them to atypical inputs, leading to degraded performance, especially in Chinese.
When causal reasoning succeeds, model representations converge toward semantically aligned abstractions across languages, indicating a shared understanding beyond surface form.
Attention patterns over syntactic components show consistent layerwise trends but differ in absolute weights between Chinese and English, reflecting language-specific structural biases.
The similarity of layerwise attention patterns (measured by SVCCA) correlates with reasoning accuracy across different input structures and languages.
papers.limitation:
Focuses exclusively on Chinese and English, representing only a small portion of the world's linguistic diversity.
Does not encompass all model architectures or training paradigms.
Primarily focuses on attention patterns and hidden representations; does not incorporate additional interpretability methods.
future_direction: Extending BICAUSE to a broader set of languages.
Advancing research on multilingual interpretability and alignment mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Language is not only a tool for communication but also a medium for human cognition and reasoning. If, as linguistic relativity suggests, the structure of language shapes cognitive patterns, then large language models (LLMs) trained on human language may also internalize the habitual logical structures embedded in different languages. To examine this hypothesis, we introduce BICAUSE, a structured bilingual dataset for causal reasoning, which includes semantically aligned Chinese and English samples in both forward and reversed causal forms. Our study reveals three key findings: (1) LLMs exhibit typologically aligned attention patterns, focusing more on causes and sentence-initial connectives in Chinese, while showing a more balanced distribution in English. (2) Models internalize language-specific preferences for causal word order and often rigidly apply them to atypical inputs, leading to degraded performance, especially in Chinese. (3) When causal reasoning succeeds, model representations converge toward semantically aligned abstractions across languages, indicating a shared understanding beyond surface form. Overall, these results suggest that LLMs not only mimic surface linguistic forms but also internalize the reasoning biases shaped by language. Rooted in cognitive linguistic theory, this phenomenon is for the first time empirically verified through structural analysis of model internals.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words
papers.research_question: Can a language model learn to express calibrated uncertainty about its own answers in natural language, and how does this compare to uncertainty from model logits?
papers.core_contribution: GPT-3 can learn to express calibrated uncertainty about its own answers in natural language, and this calibration generalizes under distribution shift.
papers.conclusion: GPT-3 can learn to express calibrated uncertainty in natural language, and this ability generalizes under distribution shift, indicating that models can be honest about their epistemic state.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-3 can be fine-tuned to produce verbalized probabilities that are calibrated.
Verbalized probability generalizes reasonably well to out-of-distribution tasks (Multi-answer and Multiply-divide).
Verbalized probability is not simply reproducing the model's logits.
The model's ability to generalize calibration relies on pre-existing latent representations that correlate with epistemic uncertainty.
Few-shot learning with 50 examples can achieve calibration close to fine-tuned models.
papers.limitation:
The training and evaluation sets differed in label distribution but not much in content and format of questions.
The study used supervised learning, which is less flexible than reinforcement learning.
future_direction: Test whether calibration generalizes to other subject areas (e.g., history or biology) and formats (e.g., chat, long-form QA).
Test language models other than GPT-3.
Explore reinforcement learning for training verbalized probability.
papers.abstract: We show that a GPT-3 model can learn to express uncertainty about its own answers in natural language -- without use of model logits. When given a question, the model generates both an answer and a level of confidence (e.g. "90% confidence" or "high confidence"). These levels map to probabilities that are well calibrated. The model also remains moderately calibrated under distribution shift, and is sensitive to uncertainty in its own answers, rather than imitating human examples. To our knowledge, this is the first time a model has been shown to express calibrated uncertainty about its own answers in natural language. For testing calibration, we introduce the CalibratedMath suite of tasks. We compare the calibration of uncertainty expressed in words ("verbalized probability") to uncertainty extracted from model logits. Both kinds of uncertainty are capable of generalizing calibration under distribution shift. We also provide evidence that GPT-3's ability to generalize calibration depends on pre-trained latent representations that correlate with epistemic uncertainty over its answers.

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Thinking Language Models via Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: Can reasoning behaviors in thinking language models be controlled using steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that reasoning behaviors in thinking LLMs are mediated by linear directions in the activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors extracted via difference of means and attribution patching.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a practical method for controlling reasoning behaviors in thinking models, opening new possibilities for fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Thinking models exhibit distinct reasoning behaviors such as backtracking, uncertainty estimation, and example testing.
These behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space.
Steering vectors extracted via difference of means can control these behaviors, increasing or decreasing their occurrence.
The steering approach works across different model architectures within the DeepSeek-R1-Distill family.
The method provides a practical tool for modulating reasoning capabilities in thinking models.
papers.limitation:
The automated annotation process using GPT-4o has occasionally produced false positives and false negatives in identifying reasoning patterns.
The generalization of these findings to other models that have undergone reward-based RL training instead of being fine-tuned on thinking models remains an open question.
future_direction: Developing more robust annotation methods, potentially incorporating multiple models or human validation.
Extending the research to a broader range of models to understand the universality of thinking mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to the development of thinking language models that generate extensive internal reasoning chains before producing responses. While these models achieve improved performance, controlling their reasoning processes remains challenging. This work presents a steering approach for thinking LLMs by analyzing and manipulating specific reasoning behaviors in DeepSeek-R1-Distill models. Through a systematic experiment on 500 tasks across 10 diverse categories, we identify several reasoning behaviors exhibited by thinking models, including expressing uncertainty, generating examples for hypothesis validation, and backtracking in reasoning chains. We demonstrate that these behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors. By extracting and applying these vectors, we provide a method to modulate specific aspects of the model's reasoning process, such as its tendency to backtrack or express uncertainty. Our approach offers practical tools for steering reasoning processes in thinking models in a controlled and interpretable manner. We validate our steering method using three DeepSeek-R1-Distill models, demonstrating consistent control across different model architectures.

papers.title: Compositional Processing Emerges in Neural Networks Solving Math Problems
papers.research_question: Do deep neural networks evaluate arithmetic expressions using the principle of compositionality by encoding and combining partial results?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on math problems can encode partial results of sub-expressions in their internal representations, demonstrating emergent compositional processing.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can exhibit compositional processing when trained on math problems, though imperfectly, suggesting a blend of compositional and holistic strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode digit quantities in their representations, with vectors organized by numerical value.
Operators encode intermediate arithmetic results, with vector distances correlating with value differences.
These encodings are found in attention vectors, indicating compositional processing.
Compositionality is imperfect, as shown by non-zero correlations across sequences.
Both standard and TP-Transformers exhibit similar patterns of compositional encoding.
papers.limitation:
The observed compositionality is imperfect, with non-zero correlations indicating incomplete separation of sub-expressions.
Models show poor generalization on extrapolation problems with different surface features.
future_direction: Clarify whether scaling leads to human-level compositionality or if explicit design is needed.
papers.abstract: A longstanding question in cognitive science concerns the learning mechanisms underlying compositionality in human cognition. Humans can infer the structured relationships (e.g., grammatical rules) implicit in their sensory observations (e.g., auditory speech), and use this knowledge to guide the composition of simpler meanings into complex wholes. Recent progress in artificial neural networks has shown that when large models are trained on enough linguistic data, grammatical structure emerges in their representations. We extend this work to the domain of mathematical reasoning, where it is possible to formulate precise hypotheses about how meanings (e.g., the quantities corresponding to numerals) should be composed according to structured rules (e.g., order of operations). Our work shows that neural networks are not only able to infer something about the structured relationships implicit in their training data, but can also deploy this knowledge to guide the composition of individual meanings into composite wholes.

papers.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully explain the model's actual reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes tests for measuring faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning and finds that faithfulness varies across tasks and model sizes, with smaller models often producing more faithful reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning is not always faithful, but it can be faithful under carefully chosen circumstances such as model size and task. Smaller models may be better to use if faithful reasoning is important.
papers.key_findings:
Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer.
CoT's performance boost does not come from added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT.
As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks studied.
Smaller models often generate more faithful reasoning than larger, more capable ones.
Faithfulness depends on model size and task difficulty, with easier tasks and larger models leading to less faithful reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Lack of ground truth about the model's internal reasoning process, making it impossible to know if CoT is truly faithful.
Analysis limited to RLHF-finetuned models; faithfulness may differ for pretrained LLMs or other training schemes.
future_direction: Investigate training schemes different from RLHF for eliciting more faithful reasoning.
Use the proposed metrics to increase the faithfulness of CoT and build systems with trustworthy reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform better when they produce step-by-step, "Chain-of-Thought" (CoT) reasoning before answering a question, but it is unclear if the stated reasoning is a faithful explanation of the model's actual reasoning (i.e., its process for answering the question). We investigate hypotheses for how CoT reasoning may be unfaithful, by examining how the model predictions change when we intervene on the CoT (e.g., by adding mistakes or paraphrasing it). Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer, sometimes relying heavily on the CoT and other times primarily ignoring it. CoT's performance boost does not seem to come from CoT's added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT. As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks we study. Overall, our results suggest that CoT can be faithful if the circumstances such as the model size and task are carefully chosen.

papers.title: Probing Latent Knowledge Conflict for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How can we improve contextual faithfulness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems by moving beyond black-box interventions and analyzing the model's internal reasoning process? Specifically, how is conflict represented in the model's latent space and how does it disrupt faithful generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ProbeRAG, a framework that leverages latent probing to detect knowledge conflicts in the model's hidden states and uses conflict-aware attention modulation to improve contextual faithfulness in RAG systems.
papers.conclusion: ProbeRAG effectively improves contextual faithfulness in RAG by moving beyond black-box interventions to internal guidance, demonstrating consistent and robust performance across various models and datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Conflicting and aligned knowledge states are linearly separable in the model's latent space, providing a detectable 'conflict feature'.
Contextual noise systematically increases the entropy of these representations, obscuring the conflict feature.
ProbeRAG, which integrates fine-grained knowledge pruning, latent conflict probing, and conflict-aware attention, substantially improves accuracy and contextual faithfulness across multiple benchmarks and models.
The accuracy of the conflict probe is positively correlated with the model's ability to generate faithful responses.
Attention visualization shows that after training with the attention-guidance loss, the model allocates more attention to tokens marked as conflicting knowledge.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful paradigm to enhance the factuality of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing RAG systems often suffer from an unfaithfulness issue, where the model's response contradicts evidence from the retrieved context. Existing approaches to improving contextual faithfulness largely rely on external interventions, such as prompt engineering, decoding constraints, or reward-based fine-tuning. These works treat the LLM as a black box and overlook a crucial question: how does the LLM internally integrate retrieved evidence with its parametric memory, particularly under knowledge conflicts? To address this gap, we conduct a probing-based analysis of hidden-state representations in LLMs and observe three findings: knowledge integration occurs hierarchically, conflicts manifest as latent signals at the sentence level, and irrelevant context is often amplified when aligned with parametric knowledge. Building on these findings, we propose CLEAR (Conflict-Localized and Enhanced Attention for RAG), a framework that (i) decomposes context into fine-grained sentence-level knowledge, (ii) employs hidden-state probing to localize conflicting knowledge, and (iii) introduces conflict-aware fine-tuning to guide the model to accurately integrate retrieved evidence. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate that CLEAR substantially improves both accuracy and contextual faithfulness, consistently outperforming strong baselines under diverse conflict conditions. The related resources are available at https://github.com/LinfengGao/CLEAR.

papers.title: Interpreting and Mitigating Unwanted Uncertainty in LLMs
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms cause LLMs to flip from correct to incorrect answers under re-evaluation, and how can we intervene to mitigate this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a small set of non-retrieval attention heads that cause unwanted uncertainty in LLMs and shows that targeted masking of these heads reduces flip behavior by up to 15% without harming baseline accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Unwanted uncertainty in LLMs is not a byproduct of retrieval failure, but rather a consequence of specific attention heads that influence decision-making under re-evaluation; masking these heads can reduce flip behavior while preserving overall accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Retrieval heads are not primarily responsible for avoiding uncertainty.
A small set of non-retrieval attention heads disproportionately attend to misleading tokens in uncertain contexts.
Masking these heads reduces flip behavior by up to 15% without introducing incoherence or overcorrection.
Masking uncertainty heads is effective only in cases of low uncertainty and can lead to overconfidence in incorrect answers in high-uncertainty tasks.
There exist some non-retrieval heads responsible for coherent outputs.
papers.limitation: Masking uncertainty heads can increase overconfidence in incorrect predictions in high-uncertainty tasks.
future_direction: Generalization to other models, architectures, and tasks.
Identifying and characterizing heads that yield incoherent outputs.
Better uncertainty head detection by analyzing attention head output vectors.
papers.abstract: Despite their impressive capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit unwanted uncertainty, a phenomenon where a model changes a previously correct answer into an incorrect one when re-prompted. This behavior undermines trust and poses serious risks in high-stakes domains. In this work, we investigate the mechanisms that drive this phenomenon. We adapt the Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval framework and integrate a Flip-style re-evaluation prompt to simulate realistic answer-flipping scenarios. We find that retrieval heads are not primarily responsible for avoiding uncertainty. Instead, we identify a small set of non-retrieval attention heads that disproportionately attend to misleading tokens in uncertain contexts. Masking these heads yields significant improvements, reducing flip behavior by up to 15% without introducing incoherence or overcorrection. However, when tested for downstream tasks, we observe trade-offs with flip behavior. Our findings contribute to the growing field of mechanistic interpretability and present a simple yet effective technique for mitigating uncertainty-driven failure modes in LLMs.

papers.title: Unveiling Internal Reasoning Modes in LLMs: A Deep Dive into Latent Reasoning vs. Factual Shortcuts with Attribute Rate Ratio
papers.research_question: How do latent reasoning and factual shortcuts differ during inference in LLMs for multi-hop questions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Attribute Rate Ratio (ARR) metric to efficiently distinguish between latent reasoning and factual shortcuts in LLMs, and provides an analysis of internal mechanisms showing that latent reasoning encodes bridge-related information while factual shortcuts bypass intermediate steps.
papers.conclusion: The work systematically investigates distinctions between latent reasoning and factual shortcuts, proposes the ARR metric for efficient classification, and demonstrates its application in RAG conflict scenarios, deepening understanding of model reasoning pathways.
papers.key_findings:
Subject representations differ significantly between reasoning modes: latent reasoning encodes bridge-related information for final answer extraction, while factual shortcuts bypass intermediate reasoning and resemble single-hop factual queries.
The proposed Attribute Rate Ratio (ARR) achieves around 90% accuracy in classifying reasoning modes on constructed datasets.
Model behavior under conflicting prompts in RAG scenarios is closely tied to its underlying reasoning mode, with latent reasoning more influenced by external context and factual shortcuts more robust to disruptive information.
The model undergoes two disjointed stages during multi-hop reasoning: local shallow reasoning (encoding relation-related attributes) and deep reasoning (integrating information for final answer).
Bridge-related information propagated from the subject position plays a decisive role in second-hop reasoning for latent reasoning modes.
papers.limitation:
Scope limited to two-hop reasoning, which may not generalize to more complex reasoning chains.
Limited dataset availability for studying latent reasoning due to many shortcut mappings in training data.
Latent multi-hop reasoning pathway identification relies on CoT filtering, which may not fully correspond to the model's internal reasoning processes.
The proposed metric lacks rigorous verification due to model complexity and limited datasets.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex reasoning beyond two-hop tasks.
Further refinement and verification of the ARR metric.
Investigating the balance between external information utilization and robustness in RAG conflicts.
papers.abstract: Yiran Yang, Haifeng Sun, Jingyu Wang, Qi Qi, Zirui Zhuang, Huazheng Wang, Pengfei Ren, Jing Wang, Jianxin Liao. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box: A Survey on the Mechanisms of Multi-Step Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that enable multi-step reasoning in large language models, covering both implicit (latent) and explicit (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) reasoning paradigms?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying multi-step reasoning in large language models, organizing existing research around seven interconnected research questions and highlighting future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes by highlighting five open research directions for future mechanistic understanding of multi-step reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs is an orchestrated, layered process with distinct modules specializing in different phases, but it is constrained by the fixed depth of transformers.
Implicit reasoning capability emerges via grokking, a phase transition from memorization to generalization, influenced by training data distribution, data scale, and optimization biases.
LLMs frequently bypass genuine multi-step reasoning by using shortcuts, such as direct input-output associations (factual shortcuts) or surface-level heuristics (structural shortcuts).
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting activates a 'reasoning mode' where models use generated tokens as external memory, breaking the depth limitation and enhancing computational expressiveness and generalization.
CoT does not equate to faithful explainability; it often functions as post-hoc rationalization due to a structural mismatch between the distributed, parallel computation of transformers and the sequential nature of explicit reasoning.
future_direction: Rigorous causal analysis in real-world settings
Bridging the faithfulness gap of explicit CoT reasoning
Mechanistic understanding of Latent CoT reasoning
White-box evaluation metrics for LLM reasoning
From mechanistic interpretation to model control
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to solve problems requiring multiple reasoning steps, yet the internal mechanisms enabling such capabilities remain elusive. Unlike existing surveys that primarily focus on engineering methods to enhance performance, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying LLM multi-step reasoning. We organize the survey around a conceptual framework comprising seven interconnected research questions, from how LLMs execute implicit multi-hop reasoning within hidden activations to how verbalized explicit reasoning remodels the internal computation. Finally, we highlight five research directions for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: Feature Hedging: Correlated Features Break Narrow Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Why do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) underperform relative to other techniques, and can we fix the problems? Specifically, the paper investigates the problem of 'feature hedging' in narrow SAEs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies 'feature hedging' as a fundamental problem in narrow sparse autoencoders (SAEs) where correlated features are merged, degrading monosemanticity, and proposes an improved variant called balance matryoshka SAEs to mitigate this issue.
papers.conclusion: Feature hedging is a core theoretical problem in SAEs that contributes to their underperformance, and the proposed balance matryoshka SAE architecture is a step towards addressing both hedging and absorption, though both problems remain.
papers.key_findings:
Feature hedging occurs when an SAE is too narrow to represent all underlying features and features are correlated, causing the SAE to merge components of correlated features into single latents.
Hedging is caused by the reconstruction (MSE) loss and becomes more severe the narrower the SAE.
In LLM SAEs, hedging is likely the norm due to the high number of correlated features and the SAE being narrower than the number of underlying features.
Balance matryoshka SAEs, which tune the relative loss coefficients between inner and outer levels, can improve performance by better balancing the competing forces of hedging and absorption.
SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging, while wider SAEs suffer more from absorption.
papers.limitation: Only test hedging in SAEs up to 65k latents on LLMs with 2b parameters due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Improving balance matryoshka SAEs by learning different balancing coefficients per latent rather than a single coefficient for all latents.
papers.abstract: It is assumed that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose polysemantic activations into interpretable linear directions, as long as the activations are composed of sparse linear combinations of underlying features. However, we find that if an SAE is more narrow than the number of underlying "true features" on which it is trained, and there is correlation between features, the SAE will merge components of correlated features together, thus destroying monosemanticity. In LLM SAEs, these two conditions are almost certainly true. This phenomenon, which we call feature hedging, is caused by SAE reconstruction loss, and is more severe the narrower the SAE. In this work, we introduce the problem of feature hedging and study it both theoretically in toy models and empirically in SAEs trained on LLMs. We suspect that feature hedging may be one of the core reasons that SAEs consistently underperform supervised baselines. Finally, we use our understanding of feature hedging to propose an improved variant of matryoshka SAEs. Importantly, our work shows that SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging than wider SAEs.

papers.title: State over Tokens: Characterizing the Role of Reasoning Tokens
papers.research_question: What is the functional role of reasoning tokens in LLMs, given that they are not faithful explanations of the model's reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the State over Tokens (SoT) conceptual framework, which reframes reasoning tokens as an externalized computational state that enables persistence across stateless generation cycles, explaining how they can drive correct reasoning without being faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning tokens are best understood as an externalized computational state (SoT), which resolves misconceptions about their completeness and shared meaning, and opens new research directions.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning tokens are not faithful explanations of the model's internal reasoning process.
Reasoning tokens function as an externalized computational state (SoT), the sole persistent information carrier across the model's stateless generation cycles.
The SoT view explains two common misconceptions: the misconception of completeness (tokens externalize only what is necessary for the next cycle) and the misconception of shared meaning (tokens may use model-specific encodings not interpretable by humans).
The tokens inhabit distinct ontological categories: as natural language text for human readers and as a computational substrate for the model.
The SoT framework surfaces new research questions about how LLMs encode and use state through tokens.
future_direction: How do LLMs decide what information to externalize at each cycle?
What information is actually encoded in the state at different points in the sequence?
Do they use consistent encodings across the solution of a problem and across different problems?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate reasoning tokens before their final answer to boost performance on complex tasks. While these sequences seem like human thought processes, empirical evidence reveals that they are not a faithful explanation of the model's actual reasoning process. To address this gap between appearance and function, we introduce the State over Tokens (SoT) conceptual framework. SoT reframes reasoning tokens not as a linguistic narrative, but as an externalized computational state -- the sole persistent information carrier across the model's stateless generation cycles. This explains how the tokens can drive correct reasoning without being a faithful explanation when read as text and surfaces previously overlooked research questions on these tokens. We argue that to truly understand the process that LLMs do, research must move beyond reading the reasoning tokens as text and focus on decoding them as state.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Behind the Scene: Revealing the Secrets of Pre-trained Vision-and-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained vision-and-language models work internally? Specifically, the paper investigates multimodal fusion, modality importance, cross-modal interaction, visual relations, and linguistic knowledge in these models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces VALUE, a set of probing tasks for vision-and-language models, and uses it to analyze UNITER and LXMERT, revealing that textual modality is more dominant, a subset of heads specialize in cross-modal interaction, and visual relations and linguistic knowledge are encoded.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into the inner workings of pre-trained V+L models and offers guidelines for future model design, such as preferring single-stream architecture and initializing with BERT weights.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models attend more to text than images during inference.
A subset of attention heads are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions.
Learned attention matrices show patterns coherent with latent alignment between image regions and textual words.
Attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions.
Linguistic knowledge is effectively encoded in the attention heads.
future_direction: Perform model compression via pruning attention heads based on the analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent Transformer-based large-scale pre-trained models have revolutionized vision-and-language (V+L) research. Models such as ViLBERT, LXMERT and UNITER have significantly lifted state of the art across a wide range of V+L benchmarks with joint image-text pre-training. However, little is known about the inner mechanisms that destine their impressive success. To reveal the secrets behind the scene of these powerful models, we present VALUE (Vision-And-Language Understanding Evaluation), a set of meticulously designed probing tasks (e.g., Visual Coreference Resolution, Visual Relation Detection, Linguistic Probing Tasks) generalizable to standard pre-trained V+L models, aiming to decipher the inner workings of multimodal pre-training (e.g., the implicit knowledge garnered in individual attention heads, the inherent cross-modal alignment learned through contextualized multimodal embeddings). Through extensive analysis of each archetypal model architecture via these probing tasks, our key observations are: (i) Pre-trained models exhibit a propensity for attending over text rather than images during inference. (ii) There exists a subset of attention heads that are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions. (iii) Learned attention matrix in pre-trained models demonstrates patterns coherent with the latent alignment between image regions and textual words. (iv) Plotted attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions. (v) Pure linguistic knowledge is also effectively encoded in the attention heads. These are valuable insights serving to guide future work towards designing better model architecture and objectives for multimodal pre-training.

papers.title: Circular Reasoning: Understanding Self-Reinforcing Loops in Large Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: What is the 'Circular Reasoning' failure mode in Large Reasoning Models, and how can we systematically analyze its mechanisms and predict its onset?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the 'Circular Reasoning' failure mode in Large Reasoning Models, introduces LoopBench for systematic evaluation, analyzes the mechanisms (state collapse, triggers, persistence via V-shaped attention), and proposes an early prediction method using CUSUM on hidden states.
papers.conclusion: Circular reasoning is a critical failure mode in LRMs that stems from intrinsic generation mechanisms, and the proposed analysis and prediction method provide a foundation for improving reasoning stability.
papers.key_findings:
Circular reasoning manifests as two distinct loop types: numerical loops (universal) and statement loops (prevalent in reasoning models).
LoopBench triggers significantly higher repetition rates than existing benchmarks, revealing model fragility.
The loop onset is triggered by reasoning impasses and sustained by a self-reinforcing V-shaped attention pattern.
Early prediction of statement loops is feasible by monitoring hidden state shifts with the CUSUM algorithm.
Decoding strategies mitigate but do not eliminate repetition, indicating an inherent trade-off between loop and accuracy.
papers.limitation:
LoopBench focuses on specific task patterns (high-precision arithmetic and complex recursive reasoning) and may not cover all reasoning scenarios.
The early prediction method is only validated for statement loops, not numerical loops.
The analysis is primarily conducted on open-source models, limiting generalizability to closed-source models.
future_direction: Expand LoopBench to more diverse tasks and domains.
Investigate loop mitigation strategies, such as dynamic decoding or architectural modifications.
Extend the analysis to more model architectures and scales.
papers.abstract: Despite the success of test-time scaling, Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) frequently encounter repetitive loops that lead to computational waste and inference failure. In this paper, we identify a distinct failure mode termed Circular Reasoning. Unlike traditional model degeneration, this phenomenon manifests as a self-reinforcing trap where generated content acts as a logical premise for its own recurrence, compelling the reiteration of preceding text. To systematically analyze this phenomenon, we introduce LoopBench, a dataset designed to capture two distinct loop typologies: numerical loops and statement loops. Mechanistically, we characterize circular reasoning as a state collapse exhibiting distinct boundaries, where semantic repetition precedes textual repetition. We reveal that reasoning impasses trigger the loop onset, which subsequently persists as an inescapable cycle driven by a self-reinforcing V-shaped attention mechanism. Guided by these findings, we employ the Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) algorithm to capture these precursors for early loop prediction. Experiments across diverse LRMs validate its accuracy and elucidate the stability of long-chain reasoning.

papers.title: Understanding the Language Model to Solve the Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Problem from the Perspective of Buffer Mechanism
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internally perform multi-step reasoning, and can we improve their reasoning capability based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the buffer mechanism to explain how Transformers perform multi-step reasoning and introduces RMBA, a method that adds random matrices to weight matrices to improve reasoning performance with few parameters.
papers.conclusion: The buffer mechanism is key to Transformer multi-step reasoning, and RMBA improves data efficiency on reasoning datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers employ a buffer mechanism to store intermediate results in separate buffers (matrices) for multi-step reasoning.
The buffer mechanism explains both vertical thinking (single forward pass) and horizontal thinking (Chain-of-Thought) strategies.
The model's out-of-distribution generalization is linked to the diagonal structure of kernel matrices (same-token matching).
The proposed Random Matrix-Based Algorithm (RMBA) improves data efficiency and performance on multi-step reasoning datasets.
CoT reasoning reuses buffers, reducing the difficulty of training compared to vertical thinking.
papers.limitation: Lacks in-depth theoretical analysis
future_direction: Conduct deeper theoretical modeling for multi-step reasoning
Extend buffer mechanism to other multi-step reasoning tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models have consistently struggled with complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical problem-solving. Investigating the internal reasoning mechanisms of these models can help us design better model architectures and training strategies, ultimately enhancing their reasoning capability. In this study, we constructed a symbolic multi-step reasoning task to investigate the information propagation mechanisms in Transformer models when solving the task through direct answering and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. We introduced the concept of buffer mechanism: the model stores various information in distinct buffers and selectively extracts it through the query-key matrix. We proposed a random matrix-based algorithm to enhance the model's reasoning ability. This algorithm introduces only 132 trainable parameters, yet leads to significant performance improvements on 7 multi-step reasoning datasets, including PrOntoQA, LogicAsker, and LogicInference. These findings provide new insights into understanding the large language models.

papers.title: Exploring the Hidden Reasoning Process of Large Language Models by Misleading Them
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) truly engage in task abstraction and rule-based reasoning beyond mere memorization?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Misleading Fine-Tuning (MisFT), an evaluation paradigm free from data contamination, and finds that LLMs can generalize contradictory rules to novel domains, suggesting an internal abstraction-reasoning mechanism.
papers.conclusion: MisFT provides evidence that LLMs possess human-like reasoning abilities through abstraction and rule-based reasoning, and it can serve as a tool for assessing generalization in various tasks and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can learn contradictory arithmetic rules through fine-tuning and apply them to solve math word problems, showing out-of-distribution generalization.
Larger models exhibit better generalization performance, indicating a positive correlation between model size and reasoning ability.
LLMs can generalize overloaded logical rules from formulas to natural language reasoning tasks in first-order logic.
Vision-language models (VLMs) can generalize contradictory rules learned from text to image-based arithmetic problems without seeing images during fine-tuning.
Deep layers in LLMs are crucial for abstraction and reasoning, as freezing them sharply reduces generalization accuracy on math word problems.
papers.limitation:
The paper does not pinpoint the actual circuits for abstraction and reasoning in the model's computational graph, leaving it for future work.
MisFT may cause catastrophic forgetting and is a disruptive probing method that could harm the model's general reasoning ability.
future_direction: Accurately pinpointing the circuits for abstraction and reasoning using more advanced mechanistic interpretation methods.
Applying MisFT to assess reasoning and generalization capabilities in a wider range of tasks and modalities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been able to perform various forms of reasoning tasks in a wide range of scenarios, but are they truly engaging in task abstraction and rule-based reasoning beyond mere memorization? To answer this question, we propose a novel experimental approach, Misleading Fine-Tuning (MisFT), to examine whether LLMs perform abstract reasoning by altering their original understanding of fundamental rules. In particular, by constructing datasets with math expressions or logical formulas that contradict correct principles, we fine-tune the model to learn those contradictory rules and assess its generalization ability on unseen test domains. Through a series of experiments, we find that current LLMs are capable of applying contradictory rules to solve practical math word problems and natural language reasoning tasks, implying the presence of an internal mechanism in LLMs that abstracts before reasoning.

papers.title: Neural Natural Language Inference Models Partially Embed Theories of Lexical Entailment and Negation
papers.research_question: Whether neural models for Natural Language Inference (NLI) can learn the compositional interactions between lexical entailment and negation.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a BERT-based model, after fine-tuning, can learn to reason about lexical entailment and negation, and structural evaluations (probes and interventions) provide evidence that the model partially embeds the target monotonicity algorithm.
papers.conclusion: The BERT model at least partially embeds a theory of lexical entailment and negation at an algorithmic level, in addition to achieving the correct input-output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on general-purpose NLI datasets (SNLI/MNLI) fail systematically on examples requiring negation to reverse lexical entailment.
Fine-tuning on a subset of the MoNLI dataset enables models to solve a systematic generalization task requiring lexical entailment and negation.
Probing experiments show that BERT's internal representations correlate with the lexical entailment relation and the algorithm's output.
Interchange intervention experiments show that BERT's causal dynamics mirror the monotonicity algorithm on specific subsets of the MoNLI data.
papers.limitation:
The interchange intervention methodology is not yet formally grounded.
The analysis only shows that BERT mimics the algorithm on subsets of MoNLI, not on the entire dataset.
papers.abstract: We address whether neural models for Natural Language Inference (NLI) can learn the compositional interactions between lexical entailment and negation, using four methods: the behavioral evaluation methods of (1) challenge test sets and (2) systematic generalization tasks, and the structural evaluation methods of (3) probes and (4) interventions. To facilitate this holistic evaluation, we present Monotonicity NLI (MoNLI), a new naturalistic dataset focused on lexical entailment and negation. In our behavioral evaluations, we find that models trained on general-purpose NLI datasets fail systematically on MoNLI examples containing negation, but that MoNLI fine-tuning addresses this failure. In our structural evaluations, we look for evidence that our top-performing BERT-based model has learned to implement the monotonicity algorithm behind MoNLI. Probes yield evidence consistent with this conclusion, and our intervention experiments bolster this, showing that the causal dynamics of the model mirror the causal dynamics of this algorithm on subsets of MoNLI. This suggests that the BERT model at least partially embeds a theory of lexical entailment and negation at an algorithmic level.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
